about.headline: Change you can
about.lead: Less dependency. Better decisions. Software people actually use. Three changes I helped teams deliver.

identity.label: About Han Che
identity.name: Han Che
identity.body: I connect the commercial, technical and human sides of change. Engineer, team lead and trainer, with 2,000+ hours of coaching and training.

about.readingKey: Read each case: before → intervention → result
about.contactTitle: Where is the work getting stuck?
about.closing: Start with the people, the process and the tools. Not another tool in isolation.
about.provenance: Selected first-person accounts, cross-checked against my CV and professional profile. These describe my contribution within teams, not independently audited results.

rib.title: A team that doesn't wait for its manager.

before.title: One gatekeeper
before.caption: Every decision queued behind one person.
before.body: Refinement, estimates, assignments and reviews converged on one gatekeeper. The team had too little ownership to move independently.

intervention.title: Shared decisions
intervention.caption: Shared planning, capacity and peer review.
intervention.body: I coached shared refinement and estimation, made capacity explicit and built peer review. Team members took responsibility for planning and their own Scrum rituals.

result.title: Independent team
result.caption: The team ran its own Scrum in ~5 months.
result.body: In ~5 months, the team was running its own Scrum rituals with little need for me to be in the room. Distributed ownership became daily practice.

rib.scope: About five months of team development. “Runs itself” refers to day-to-day team routines, not an organisation without leadership.
rib.note: My intervention was not another approval layer. I helped the team refine and estimate together, communicate its capacity and unblock work with other teams. Peer review gave colleagues a way to build agreement and carry decisions themselves.
rib.source: Basis: personal accomplishment notes; Engineering Manager role and five-month transformation recorded in my CV.

audi.title: Less meeting. More deciding.
audi.unit: minutes saved per meeting, on average

before.title: Legacy approval
before.caption: Brief: rebuild the Excel approval flow.
before.body: The final approval before serial production depended on a legacy process. The starting request was to reproduce the existing Excel workflow.

intervention.title: Model the process
intervention.caption: Stakeholder sessions became a state model.
intervention.body: With an architect colleague, I worked through stakeholder sessions, state diagrams and a relational data model. We built one core process end to end.

result.title: Digital sign-off
result.caption: A core-process demo, meetings 30 min shorter.
result.body: The core-process demo made the model tangible. The digitisation effort also shortened approval meetings by an average of 30 minutes.

audi.scope: 6–8 weeks refers to the working core-process demo. The initial release took 6 months. The 30-minute figure is the average meeting reduction, not a demo benchmark.
audi.note: State transitions gave stakeholders a model in their own domain language. The demo ran on pre-production with data import and export, side by side with the existing tool. It was a concrete basis for agreement on how the process should work.
audi.source: Basis: personal accomplishment notes for the demo; CV for the six-month initial release and average meeting reduction.

selfbits.title: Beyond the demo. Into production.

before.title: Production data
before.caption: Orders needed to become usable OEE data.
before.body: How can production orders become usable data about equipment effectiveness? The work needed to connect manufacturing processes with the people operating them.

intervention.title: Build and pilot
intervention.caption: Web, mobile and TV software, built and run.
intervention.body: I designed, implemented and operated manufacturing execution software with the team: web, mobile and TV interfaces for scheduling, master data and OEE.

result.title: Software in use
result.caption: 200+ users, 3 HEPA lines piloted in 9 months.
result.body: The software served 200+ users across the total deployment. A defined pilot acquired order-based OEE data on 3 HEPA lines in 2 factories within 9 months.

selfbits.scope: 5 factories and 200+ users describe the total deployment in my CV. The nine-month milestone covers the 3-line, 2-factory pilot, not the full rollout.
selfbits.note: Manufacturing execution software connects production planning with work on the factory floor. OEE means overall equipment effectiveness. Here, the pilot concerned acquiring that data per production order; no percentage improvement in OEE is claimed.
selfbits.source: Basis: CV for deployment and pilot scope; professional profile for work on scheduling, OEE dashboards and master data.

amnesiac-freelancer.title: Treat AI like an amnesiac freelancer you have to onboard
amnesiac-freelancer.caption: Why an AI coding agent starts every session blank, and how to brief it so the work still lands.
amnesiac-freelancer.description: An AI coding agent keeps nothing between sessions. Treat it like a skilled freelancer who forgets: brief it in files, keep the brief short, and verify the work.

blank-slate.title: The freelancer who forgets
blank-slate.caption: Why the agent arrives with no memory of your project, and where its knowledge does and does not live.

blank-every-time.title: Why every session starts from a blank slate
blank-every-time.caption: “Amnesiac” is our metaphor, not a vendor term, but the mechanism is documented.

demo.caption: Each session fills up, then starts over blank.

blank-every-time.prose: The model <ref>keeps nothing between requests</ref>: a chat only feels continuous because the history is sent again every turn. Claude Code says each session begins with a fresh context window. Anthropic itself pictures engineers working in shifts, each arriving with no memory of the previous shift.

stateless-by-design.description: The model keeps nothing between requests.[2] A chat feels continuous because the whole history is sent again each turn.[1]

fresh-window-per-session.description: Claude Code says each session begins with a fresh context window.[1] Only CLAUDE.md files and auto memory carry knowledge across.

shift-workers-per-anthropic.description: Anthropic pictures engineers in shifts, each arriving with no memory of the previous shift.[1] Their fix is written artefacts the next session reads first.

anthropic-long-running-harnesses.title: Anthropic: Effective harnesses for long-running agents

our-word-not-theirs.description: "Amnesiac" is our metaphor. Say so out loud; do not attribute it to Anthropic.

blank-slate.title: Blank slate
blank-slate.script: Start with the uncomfortable fact. The model keeps nothing between requests. When a chat feels like a conversation, that is because the whole history is sent again with every turn. Nothing was remembered; it was re-read.

new-session-new-window.title: New session, new window
new-session-new-window.keywords: fresh context window, CLAUDE.md, auto memory
new-session-new-window.script: Claude Code's own documentation says each session begins with a fresh context window. Only two things cross the gap: instruction files like CLAUDE.md, and notes the agent wrote down. Both are just text loaded at the start.

shifts.title: Shifts
shifts.keywords: engineers in shifts, no memory, written artefacts
shifts.script: Anthropic describes it as engineers working in shifts, each new one arriving with no memory of the last. I call it an amnesiac freelancer. That word is mine, not theirs, but the mechanism is theirs. And their answer is the same as ours: write it down.
shifts.bridge: So if the agent knows nothing about us, where does what it does know come from?

where-knowledge-lives.title: Where an agent’s knowledge lives, and where it stops
where-knowledge-lives.caption: Three places, and only one of them is yours to shape.

training.title: Training
training.prose: General knowledge up to a cutoff date. Your repo, your conventions and last Tuesday’s decision were never part of it. That is our framing; vendors point to files for exactly this reason.

session.title: The session
session.prose: The context window is its working memory. Recall degrades as it fills, and information buried in the middle of a long input is used worst.

files.title: Files
files.prose: CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md are loaded as text at the start. A project-root CLAUDE.md is re-read from disk after compaction; an instruction given only in chat can be lost.

training.description: General knowledge up to a cutoff. Your repo, conventions and last Tuesday's decision were never in it. That is our inference; no vendor states it as a sentence, but vendor guidance points to files for exactly this reason.[1][2]

the-session.description: The context window is working memory. Recall degrades as it fills (Anthropic, Chroma).[1][3] Information in the middle of a long input is used worst (Liu et al., 2023-era models; state the direction, not numbers).[2]

lost-in-the-middle.title: Liu et al.: Lost in the Middle

anthropic-context-engineering.title: Anthropic: Effective context engineering for AI agents

files.description: CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md are loaded as text at the start.[1] A project-root CLAUDE.md is re-read from disk after /compact; instructions given only in chat can be lost.[2]

claude-code-how-it-works.title: Claude Code: How Claude Code works

compaction-is-lossy.description: Anthropic warns aggressive compaction can drop subtle but critical context.[1] The research did not quantify the loss.

anthropic-context-engineering.title: Anthropic: Effective context engineering for AI agents

training.title: Training
training.script: First place: training. It is broad and it stops at a cutoff date. It never saw your repository, your naming rules, or the decision you made last Tuesday. To be fair, that is my framing rather than a vendor quote, but every vendor tells you to put project context in files, and that is why.

the-session.title: The session
the-session.script: Second place: the session. The context window is the agent's working memory. Anthropic and an independent report from Chroma both find that recall gets worse as it fills. And the Lost in the Middle paper found that what sits in the middle of a long input is used worst. That study used older models, so take the direction, not the numbers.

files.title: Files
files.keywords: CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, compaction, re-read from disk
files.script: Third place: files. This is the only one you control. CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md are loaded as text at the start. After a compaction, the project-root CLAUDE.md is read from disk again, while something you only said in chat may be gone.
files.bridge: So files are the lever. Next: what goes in them. Think of it as onboarding.

onboarding.title: Onboarding the newcomer
onboarding.caption: {count, plural, one {# slide} other {# slides}} on briefing an agent the way you would brief a skilled contractor.

brief-and-rules.title: What a good onboarding package contains
brief-and-rules.caption: Each human artefact has an agent counterpart.

brief.title: The brief
brief.prose: Anthropic: think of Claude as a brilliant but new employee who lacks context on your norms and workflows. State the task, constraints and format explicitly.

house-rules.title: House rules
house-rules.prose: A file read at the start of every conversation: build and test commands, code style, workflow rules. AGENTS.md calls it a README for agents.

definition-of-done.title: Definition of done
definition-of-done.prose: Tests, builds or scripts the agent can run itself. Anthropic: give Claude a way to verify its work.

the-brief.description: Anthropic: "Think of Claude as a brilliant but new employee who lacks context on your norms and workflows."[1] Be explicit; "above and beyond" must be requested, not inferred.

claude-be-clear-and-direct.title: Claude docs: Be clear and direct

house-rules.description: A file read at the start of every conversation: commands, code style, workflow rules.[1] agents.md calls it a "README for agents"; the nearest file wins.[2]

definition-of-done.description: Give the agent a way to verify its work: tests, scripts, screenshots.[1] Also GitHub: say how to build and validate so the agent need not search each time.[2]

github-copilot-repository-instructions.title: GitHub Docs: Adding repository custom instructions for Copilot

colleague-test.description: Show your prompt to a colleague with minimal context; if they would be confused, Claude will be too.[1]

claude-be-clear-and-direct.title: Claude docs: Be clear and direct

the-brief.title: The brief
the-brief.keywords: brilliant new employee, explicit, colleague test
the-brief.script: Anthropic itself uses this frame: a brilliant but new employee who lacks context on your norms and workflows. So write the brief like that. Task, constraints, format. And try the colleague test: hand it to someone with no context. If they would be confused, so will the agent.

house-rules.title: House rules
house-rules.keywords: README for agents, every conversation, commands
house-rules.script: House rules live in a file the agent reads at the start of every conversation. Build and test commands, code style, workflow rules. The agents.md site calls it a README for agents. And the closest file to the code wins, like asking the old hand in that corner of the codebase.

definition-of-done.title: Definition of done
definition-of-done.script: The third item matters most. Give the agent a way to verify its work. A test it can run, a command that must pass. Without that it cannot tell whether it is done, and neither can you.
definition-of-done.bridge: Now the temptation: put everything in. Why that backfires.

keep-it-short.title: Why a short brief beats a thorough handbook
keep-it-short.caption: Attention is finite, for agents and humans alike.
keep-it-short.prose: Anthropic warns that <ref>bloated CLAUDE.md files cause Claude to ignore your actual instructions</ref>, and suggests under 200 lines per file. GitHub caps its own template at two pages. Point to detail the agent can load on demand instead of pasting it all in.

bloat-gets-ignored.description: Anthropic: "Bloated CLAUDE.md files cause Claude to ignore your actual instructions."[1] Pruning test: would removing this line cause mistakes?

numbers-to-cite.description: Under 200 lines per CLAUDE.md file (Anthropic).[1] GitHub's template caps instructions at 2 pages.[2]

github-copilot-repository-instructions.title: GitHub Docs: Adding repository custom instructions for Copilot

minimal-is-not-short.description: "Minimal does not necessarily mean short": the smallest set that fully outlines the behaviour.[1] Prefer pointers loaded on demand over pastes. Imports do not save context.[2]

anthropic-context-engineering.title: Anthropic: Effective context engineering for AI agents

more-is-worse.title: More is worse
more-is-worse.script: The instinct is to write the complete handbook. Anthropic's advice is the opposite: bloated CLAUDE.md files cause Claude to ignore your actual instructions. Their guideline is under 200 lines per file, and GitHub caps its own template at two pages.

prune.title: Prune
prune.keywords: would removing this cause mistakes, pointers
prune.script: Use the pruning question: would removing this line cause a mistake? If not, cut it. And point instead of paste: a path the agent can open when it needs it costs nothing until then.

minimal-is-not-short.title: Minimal is not short
minimal-is-not-short.script: One caution from Anthropic. Minimal does not mean short. It means the smallest set that fully outlines what you expect. Enough, not everything.
minimal-is-not-short.bridge: One kind of content always earns its place: the why behind decisions.

decisions-in-writing.title: Why decisions belong in writing
decisions-in-writing.caption: Write each one as a conversation with a future developer.
decisions-in-writing.prose: Michael Nygard’s decision records keep the why for whoever arrives later, in one or two pages, and <ref>mark a reversed decision as superseded instead of deleting it</ref>. For an agent that arrives later every time, the record is the memory it can read.

a-conversation-with-a-future-developer.header: A conversation with a future developer
a-conversation-with-a-future-developer.description: Nygard's rule for decision records.[1] Short prose, one or two pages.

superseded-not-deleted.description: A reversed decision is kept and marked superseded.[1]

the-newcomers-two-bad-options.description: Without the record, the newcomer must blindly accept or blindly change a decision.[1]

mapping-not-a-sourced-claim.description: That an agent reads the same record is our mapping. No vendor page quoted says so.

why-it-was-done.title: Why it was done
why-it-was-done.script: Michael Nygard wrote decision records for exactly this person: someone who arrives later. His rule: write each one as if it is a conversation with a future developer. One or two pages, plain prose.

superseded.title: Superseded
superseded.keywords: keep the old one, mark superseded
superseded.script: When you reverse a decision, keep the old record and mark it superseded. Without any record, the newcomer has two bad options: accept the decision blindly, or change it blindly.

our-agent-arrives-later-every-time.title: Our agent arrives later, every time
our-agent-arrives-later-every-time.script: Our freelancer is always the newcomer. That is my mapping, not a vendor claim, but it follows: for someone who arrives later every single time, the written record is the only memory they can read.
our-agent-arrives-later-every-time.bridge: We have a decent onboarding package. Now where the freelancer picture misleads us.

where-it-breaks.title: Where the metaphor breaks
where-it-breaks.caption: Three differences between a freelancer and an agent, and what follows from them.

metaphor-breaks.title: Three ways an agent is not a freelancer
metaphor-breaks.caption: Each difference changes how you onboard.

no-learning.title: No learning
no-learning.prose: A freelancer improves by week three unprompted. A fresh session starts from the files alone, so anything not written down is gone.

not-enforced.title: Not enforced
not-enforced.prose: Claude treats CLAUDE.md as context, not enforced configuration. Rules that must hold belong in checks or hooks, not prose.

reading-costs.title: Reading costs
reading-costs.prose: Every line is paid for at the start of every session, and quality drops as context fills. Prune the brief.

no-learning.description: A freelancer improves by week three unprompted.[1] A fresh session starts from files alone. Auto memory narrows the gap but it is saved notes loaded at start, not learning.

context-not-enforcement.description: "Claude treats them as context, not enforced configuration."[1] Hard rules need hooks, permissions or checks.

reading-costs.description: The agent pays for every line at every session start, and "performance degrades as it fills".[1] Curate and prune.

beyond-the-sources.description: Silent conflicts between rules (nearest file wins, root-down concatenation) are mechanical, not negotiated.[1][2] Over-compliance is our inference, not a vendor claim.

no-learning.title: No learning
no-learning.script: First break: a freelancer gets better by week three without being told. The agent does not. Auto memory helps, but it is saved notes loaded at the start, not learning. Anything unwritten is gone.

not-enforced.title: Not enforced
not-enforced.script: Second: instructions are context, not enforced configuration. That is Anthropic's wording. Prose is a request. Anything that must always hold belongs in a check or a hook.

reading-costs.title: Reading costs
reading-costs.script: Third: reading is not free. A human skims the handbook once. The agent pays for every line at the start of every session, and quality falls as the window fills. So prune.
reading-costs.bridge: That second point has a practical consequence: who checks the work.

enforce-and-verify.title: Why checks matter more than good intentions
enforce-and-verify.caption: Let something other than the author grade the work.
enforce-and-verify.prose: Give the agent commands that prove the work, and add a fresh-context reviewer, so the agent doing the work is not the one grading it. That is the one part that does not depend on the agent reading and obeying prose.

verification-you-can-run.description: "If you can't verify it, don't ship it."[1] Tests, scripts, screenshots.

a-different-grader.description: A fresh-context reviewer, "so the agent doing the work isn't the one grading it".[1] The source supports the practice, not any claim about the agent's psychology.

independent-of-prose.description: Checks are the one part that does not depend on the agent reading and obeying text.

close.description: Write it down, keep it short, make it checkable.

prove-it.title: Prove it
prove-it.script: Give the agent commands that prove the work. Anthropic is blunt: if you can't verify it, don't ship it.

another-pair-of-eyes.title: Another pair of eyes
another-pair-of-eyes.script: And bring in a reviewer with fresh context, so the agent doing the work isn't the one grading it. I would not claim to know why an agent over-trusts itself; the practice is what the source supports.

wrap-up.title: Wrap up
wrap-up.script: Three things to take away. Write it down, because nothing carries over otherwise. Keep it short, because attention is finite. Make it checkable, because prose is only a request.
wrap-up.bridge: End of Episode. Invite the viewer to try this on one repository this week.

one-line.statement: Write it down, or the next session never knew it.

ai-token-economy.title: The AI Token Economy
ai-token-economy.caption: AI can give you and the people you lead super powers, but it comes with hidden managing responsibilities you didn't sign up for.
ai-token-economy.description: A field guide to the token economy: what AI actually costs, why the meter stays invisible, and how to manage context and models efficiently.

motivation.title: Motivation
motivation.caption: Thought experiment: Imagine you're assigned a freelancer with these weird characteristics.
motivation.prose: On paper, this collaborator arrives with encyclopedic knowledge, works instantly, and accepts tasks without hesitation. But they carry three peculiar flaws.

freelancer-metaphor.description: Translates abstract LLM mechanics into intuitive human management terms: encyclopedic knowledge, instant execution, but crucial blind spots.

management-opt-in.description: Treating an LLM as a teammate requires recognizing its failure modes rather than treating it as an infallible search oracle.

lead-one-upskill-many.title: Lead One, Upskill Many
lead-one-upskill-many.caption: It's an LLM — but if it were a human, how would you manage it?
lead-one-upskill-many.prose: Directing an AI agent requires the same delegation and review rigor as onboarding an external specialist.

upskill-vs-replace.description: The objective is not replacing workers but elevating human operators into effective directors of synthetic labor.

the-four-eras-of-ai.title: The Four Eras of AI
the-four-eras-of-ai.caption: New technology gives rise to new disciplines for humans to cope.
the-four-eras-of-ai.prose: From Prompt Engineering in 2023 to Context Engineering in 2024, Harness Engineering in 2025, and Token Economics today.

emerging-disciplines.description: As model capabilities advance, operational focus shifts from prompt words to managing context, harnesses, and token budgets.

the-invisible-invoice.title: The Invisible Invoice
the-invisible-invoice.caption: For a real freelancer you need a business case. AI just bills you.
the-invisible-invoice.prose: A €3,200 consultant invoice requires purchase orders and approvals. AI accumulates identical costs silently across thousands of micro-prompts.

governance-asymmetry.description: Corporate finance demands formal approval for contractors, yet AI charges comparable budgets without procurement gates.

outcome-per-euro.title: Outcome Per Euro
outcome-per-euro.caption: You're now accountable for a budget you never signed up to manage.
outcome-per-euro.prose: Defaulting to flagship frontier models for routine chores burns capital. The economic winner optimizes outcome per euro.

budget-accountability.description: Selecting the right tier for each task is the foundation of modern engineering leadership.

what-is-a-token.title: What Is a Token
what-is-a-token.caption: Tokens are the basic unit of data for LLMs — every one is billed.
what-is-a-token.prose: LLMs calculate statistical probabilities over numerical tokens. Every word, character, and prompt translates to billable units.

probabilistic-units.description: LLMs process numerical token IDs, not human prose. Understanding token granularity reveals where costs accumulate.

live-context-breakdown.title: Live Context Breakdown
live-context-breakdown.caption: Most tools hide the meter — this is what seeing it looks like.
live-context-breakdown.prose: A typical 200k session breakdown: system prompts, conversation history, tool payloads, and retrieved documentation.

synthetic-abstractions.description: Commercial interfaces conceal real token usage behind credits and bars. Direct transparency is essential for optimization.

cli-vs-web-tool-obscurity.title: CLI vs Web Tool Obscurity
cli-vs-web-tool-obscurity.caption: The meter is hidden on purpose.
cli-vs-web-tool-obscurity.prose: Obscurity is a product pattern: frictionless initiation, habitual workflows, and surprising monthly invoices.

the-obscurity-playbook.description: Hiding usage metrics fosters dependency before organizations realize the compounding cost of unmanaged agentic loops.

managing-context.title: Managing Context
managing-context.caption: Context window is the model's attention span.
managing-context.prose: Tokens accumulate in the context window. As the window fills, attention degrades and critical instructions slip away.

cognitive-stamina.description: Context windows behave like cognitive stamina across a long workday: alert early on, distracted as history piles up.

the-lost-middle.title: The Lost Middle
the-lost-middle.caption: How key instructions get lost in the middle.
the-lost-middle.prose: Models attend sharply to the start and end of context, but the middle blurs into an attention valley.

attention-valley.description: Research proves the U-shaped retrieval curve: information placed in the middle of long contexts suffers dramatic recall drops.

the-fullness-gauge-and-levers.title: The Fullness Gauge & Levers
the-fullness-gauge-and-levers.caption: Past ~half full, the model starts losing the plot.
the-fullness-gauge-and-levers.prose: Below 50% is the smart zone. Above 50%, accuracy degrades. Above 75%, hallucination risk spikes. Three levers: Monitor, Compact, Hand off.

smart-zone-discipline.description: Keeping context windows under 50% capacity guarantees high accuracy and prevents silent prompt drift.

cost-of-agentic-ai.title: Cost of Agentic AI
cost-of-agentic-ai.caption: One small bug fix compounds to ~73,000 tokens of context.
cost-of-agentic-ai.prose: Agentic loops re-transmit the entire conversation history on every single tool call and reflection step.

agentic-compounding.description: Each tool call and test run appends full file outputs into history, compounding input token counts exponentially.

the-compounding-cost-curve.title: The Compounding Cost Curve
the-compounding-cost-curve.caption: The same bug fix, priced across models.
the-compounding-cost-curve.prose: You are billed for tokens processed on every turn, not window capacity. A routine bug fix produces a 14× price swing across models.

the-14x-spread.description: At scale, routing identical loops between frontier and economy tiers creates a multi-thousand-dollar difference each month.

model-tiers.title: Model Tiers
model-tiers.caption: My real model stack: one workflow, many models.
model-tiers.prose: Route each phase to the most economical capable model: flat-rate chats for ideation, frontier reasoning for architecture, fast models for code execution.

tiered-stack-architecture.description: Economic fluency means matching engine cost to task risk, switching models seamlessly as project phases progress.

zero-marginal-thinking.description: Use flat-rate consumer subscriptions for exploratory chats, reserving pay-per-token frontier calls for high-leverage decisions.

tools-and-tips.title: Tools & Tips
tools-and-tips.caption: Three levers to improve your token economy
tools-and-tips.prose: Combine automated tooling (rtk, compression, linting) with structural context steering and disciplined team habits (edit don't append, session hygiene).

tooling-and-steering.description: Automated compressors prune tool payloads before they reach the model, while structured rules steer execution deterministically.

operational-habits.description: Edit flawed prompts instead of stacking corrections, clear idle sessions before cache expiry, and monitor usage via transparent CLIs.

slide-layouts.title: Slide layouts
slide-layouts.caption: Every Slide layout, one Slide each.
slide-layouts.description: A gallery of every Slide layout an Episode can use: section slide, basic page and three columns.

section-slide.title: Section slide
section-slide.caption: Title and caption, vertically centred. It opens every Section and names it.

basic-page.title: Basic page
basic-page.caption: Title and caption up top, one block of prose below.
basic-page.prose: The prose is a target a Speaker note can name, like the title and the caption.

layout-target.description: Layouts offer targets for free: title, caption and prose. Name one in a note's target and the drawer highlights it.

three-column.title: Three columns
three-column.caption: Title and caption up top, exactly three keyed columns below.

first.title: First column
first.prose: Each column has a slug, and its slug is the target a note names it by.

second.title: Second column
second.prose: Columns hold a title and prose, never a position.
